source_title: AWS EKS & Kubernetes — Decision Intelligence Knowledge Base

cleaned_entries.title: Pods — The Atomic Scheduling Unit
cleaned_entries.content:
Pods — The Atomic Scheduling Unit

A Pod is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes — a logical host for one or more tightly coupled containers sharing a network namespace and storage volumes. Pods are ephemeral by design: they can be killed, rescheduled, and replaced at any time. The AI agent must understand that pods are NEVER managed directly in production; they are always controlled by a higher-level workload controller (Deployment, StatefulSet, Job). The Pod spec defines resource requests, limits, probes, security context, and volume mounts — all of which are critical to scheduling decisions and production stability.

Decision rules:
- NEVER create raw Pods directly in production — always use a controller (Deployment, StatefulSet, Job, DaemonSet)
- USE a single-container Pod as the default pattern — multi-container pods (sidecars) only for logging agents, service mesh proxies, or config synchronizers tightly coupled to the main app
- ASSUME every Pod will be rescheduled — design applications to be stateless and re-entrant by default
- SIZE Pod resource requests based on the p95 observed CPU/memory from load tests — not guesses
- USE init containers for database migration or dependency readiness checks — run sequentially before the main container starts
- APPLY pod anti-affinity rules for critical workloads to prevent multiple replicas from landing on the same node — single node failure must not cause full outage

Trade-offs:
- Single-container pods: simplicity and debuggability vs. cannot share in-process communication with sidecars
- Multi-container pods (sidecars): powerful for service mesh, logging, auth proxy vs. increases scheduling complexity and restarts one container may kill healthy siblings
- Ephemeral pods: horizontal scalability vs. any in-memory state is lost on reschedule — forces good application design
- Init containers: clean dependency ordering vs. add startup latency — bad choice for very fast-starting apps

Anti-patterns:
- Running pods with no resource requests — Kubernetes scheduler cannot make correct node placement decisions, leads to noisy-neighbor OOM kills
- Using Pod hostNetwork: true in production — bypasses Kubernetes network isolation and makes port conflicts likely
- Storing persistent data in Pod ephemeral storage (emptyDir) and expecting it to survive restarts
- Running multiple unrelated services in a single Pod — violates single-responsibility, breaks independent scaling
- Pinning Pods to specific nodes with nodeName — bypasses scheduler, breaks cluster autoscaling

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Reliability Pillar: pod anti-affinity across AZs mirrors the multi-AZ redundancy principle of AWS Well-Architected
- Security Pillar: pod-level security context (runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem) aligns with least-privilege compute
- Performance Efficiency: right-sized resource requests enable bin-packing and Karpenter node provisioning accuracy

cleaned_entries.title: Deployments — Stateless Workload Controller
cleaned_entries.content:
Deployments — Stateless Workload Controller

A Deployment manages a ReplicaSet, which in turn manages identical Pod replicas. It is the primary controller for stateless applications. Deployments provide declarative rollout strategies, rollback capability, and replica scaling. The Deployment's spec.strategy field controls how updates are rolled out — the choice of strategy (RollingUpdate vs Recreate) has direct production availability implications. In EKS, Deployments are the default workload type for APIs, web services, background processors, and any application where all replicas are identical.

Decision rules:
- USE Deployments for ALL stateless workloads — APIs, frontends, background workers consuming from queues
- USE RollingUpdate strategy (default) for zero-downtime updates — set maxUnavailable: 0 and maxSurge: 1 for production-critical services
- USE Recreate strategy ONLY when the application cannot run two versions simultaneously (e.g., database schema lock) and a brief downtime is acceptable
- SET minReadySeconds to ensure pods are truly healthy before being counted as available — prevents premature rollout completion
- USE Deployment revisionHistoryLimit: 5 in production — enables kubectl rollout undo to any of the last 5 revisions
- SCALE Deployments horizontally (increase replicas) before scaling vertically (increase resource limits) — horizontal scaling is cheaper and faster in EKS

Trade-offs:
- RollingUpdate: zero downtime vs. two versions running simultaneously requires backward-compatible APIs
- Recreate: simple version transition vs. guaranteed downtime window during updates
- High replica count: fault tolerance and throughput vs. higher baseline cost and more complex scheduling
- Deployment vs. StatefulSet: Deployments are simpler but assume replicas are interchangeable — breaks for stateful apps

Anti-patterns:
- Using StatefulSets for stateless applications — wastes ordered pod management overhead with no benefit
- Setting maxUnavailable: 50% on single-digit replica counts — kills too many pods at once, causes partial outages
- Not setting resource limits on Deployment pods — one misbehaving deployment can starve the entire node
- Deploying with spec.replicas: 1 in production — single point of failure, no rolling update capability
- Using image tag 'latest' in Deployment spec — prevents rollback, causes non-deterministic behavior

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Reliability Pillar: RollingUpdate with maxUnavailable: 0 is the EKS-recommended pattern for zero-downtime deploys
- Operational Excellence: revision history enables rapid rollback — supports mean-time-to-recovery (MTTR) targets
- EKS Best Practices: Deployments work natively with ALB Ingress Controller and HPA for auto-scaling

cleaned_entries.title: Services — Internal Networking (ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer)
cleaned_entries.content:
Services — Internal Networking (ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer)

A Kubernetes Service provides a stable virtual IP and DNS name for a dynamic set of Pods selected by label. Services decouple consumers from the Pod lifecycle — Pods are replaced, the Service endpoint persists. There are three primary types relevant to production EKS: ClusterIP (internal only), NodePort (node-level port exposure), and LoadBalancer (provisions an AWS load balancer). On EKS, the LoadBalancer type is managed by the AWS Load Balancer Controller and provisions either ALB or NLB resources. ClusterIP is the correct default; LoadBalancer should be used sparingly.

Decision rules:
- USE ClusterIP as the default Service type for all internal microservice-to-microservice communication
- USE LoadBalancer type ONLY when the service must be directly internet-facing and an Ingress is not appropriate (e.g., TCP-level services, gRPC without HTTP/2 termination at the ALB)
- USE NodePort ONLY for local development or legacy on-premises load balancer integration — never in standard EKS production
- PREFER Ingress + ClusterIP over creating one LoadBalancer Service per application — multiple LoadBalancer services multiply NLB/ALB costs
- USE Service type ExternalName to create CNAME aliases to external services (RDS endpoint, ElastiCache) — keeps DNS resolution internal to cluster
- SET sessionAffinity: ClientIP for Services fronting stateful in-memory sessions that cannot be migrated — understand this breaks horizontal scaling

Trade-offs:
- ClusterIP: zero external cost, fully isolated vs. requires Ingress or VPN to expose externally
- LoadBalancer per service: direct L4 access, simple vs. one ALB/NLB per service = high cost at scale
- Shared Ingress + ClusterIP: cost-efficient, feature-rich routing vs. adds Ingress controller as a shared dependency
- NodePort: works without cloud integration vs. exposes arbitrary high ports, requires security group management

Anti-patterns:
- Creating a LoadBalancer Service for every microservice — at 20 services, this means 20 ALBs ($20+/month each minimum)
- Using NodePort in production without a managed load balancer in front — exposes node IPs directly
- Not setting Service port names — breaks Istio/Envoy protocol detection and metrics labeling
- Omitting selector on a Service without intentionally creating a headless service — results in a Service with no endpoints

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Cost Optimization: shared ALB via Ingress reduces per-service load balancer costs by 60-80%
- Security Pillar: ClusterIP services are not reachable from outside the VPC — reduces attack surface
- EKS Best Practices: AWS Load Balancer Controller is the recommended way to manage AWS ELB resources from Kubernetes

cleaned_entries.title: Ingress — L7 Routing, TLS Termination, and Path-Based Rules
cleaned_entries.content:
Ingress — L7 Routing, TLS Termination, and Path-Based Rules

Ingress is a Kubernetes API object that manages external HTTP/HTTPS access to Services inside the cluster. It provides L7 features: host-based routing, path-based routing, TLS termination, and header manipulation. On EKS, an Ingress is reconciled by the AWS Load Balancer Controller into an Application Load Balancer (ALB). Multiple Ingress resources can share a single ALB using IngressGroup annotations — a critical cost optimization. Ingress is the canonical entry point for HTTP workloads on EKS; using a raw LoadBalancer Service for HTTP traffic is an anti-pattern.

Decision rules:
- USE Ingress for ALL HTTP/HTTPS workloads — it maps to ALB which provides SSL termination, WAF integration, and path routing
- USE alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/group.name annotation to share one ALB across multiple Ingress resources — reduces ALB cost from O(n) to O(1)
- USE IngressClass to select between ALB (HTTP) and NLB (TCP) — choose based on protocol requirements, not preference
- TERMINATE TLS at the ALB using ACM certificates — never serve plain HTTP in production, never manage TLS certs inside pods
- USE host-based routing for multi-tenant or multi-service cluster — api.example.com and app.example.com on one ALB
- USE path-based routing (/api/*, /web/*) for monolith decomposition — enables gradual service extraction without DNS changes

Trade-offs:
- ALB Ingress: rich L7 features, WAF, native AWS integration vs. ALB provisioning takes 1-3 minutes on first apply
- Nginx Ingress Controller: battle-tested, rich annotation set vs. requires managing the controller itself as a Deployment
- Shared ALB (IngressGroup): cost-efficient vs. one misconfigured Ingress can affect all services sharing the ALB
- TLS at ALB: simpler pod config vs. traffic inside VPC is unencrypted (mitigated by VPC isolation)

Anti-patterns:
- Not using IngressGroup — results in one ALB per Ingress, 10 services = 10 ALBs = 10x ALB cost
- Handling TLS termination inside pods — complex certificate rotation, no WAF capability, no access logs in ALB
- Using wildcard path /* with a single backend — defeats the purpose of Ingress routing, better to use a LoadBalancer Service
- Deploying Ingress without readiness probe on backend pods — ALB registers unhealthy targets, returns 502 errors

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Security Pillar: ALB + ACM + WAF integration satisfies encryption-in-transit and perimeter defense requirements
- Cost Optimization: IngressGroup sharing one ALB across a service mesh is the AWS-recommended pattern
- EKS Blueprints: AWS Load Balancer Controller is a required add-on in all EKS Blueprint reference architectures

cleaned_entries.title: ConfigMaps & Secrets — Configuration Separation Strategy
cleaned_entries.content:
ConfigMaps & Secrets — Configuration Separation Strategy

ConfigMaps store non-sensitive configuration data as key-value pairs. Secrets store sensitive data (passwords, tokens, certificates) in base64-encoded form. On EKS, the production pattern is NOT to use native Kubernetes Secrets for sensitive values — because they are stored in etcd base64-encoded (not encrypted at rest unless envelope encryption is configured). The AWS-native production pattern is: store secrets in AWS Secrets Manager or SSM Parameter Store, and use the External Secrets Operator or Secrets Store CSI Driver to sync them into pods. ConfigMaps are safe for non-sensitive config and are the correct tool for application configuration injection.

Decision rules:
- USE ConfigMaps for non-sensitive configuration: feature flags, log levels, external API endpoints, connection pool sizes
- NEVER store real credentials, API keys, or passwords in ConfigMaps — even base64 values — use Secrets or better
- USE AWS Secrets Manager + External Secrets Operator (ESO) for all sensitive values in production EKS — ESO syncs ASM secrets as Kubernetes Secrets automatically
- USE Secrets Store CSI Driver when you need secrets mounted as files (TLS certs, SSH keys) without creating Kubernetes Secret objects
- ENABLE EKS envelope encryption (KMS CMK) for etcd Secrets if you must use native Kubernetes Secrets — required for compliance (PCI, HIPAA)
- MOUNT ConfigMaps as environment variables for simple key-value config; mount as volume files for multi-line config (nginx.conf, application.yaml)

Trade-offs:
- Native Kubernetes Secrets: simple, no external dependency vs. not truly encrypted without KMS envelope encryption
- External Secrets Operator: production-grade, centralized secret management vs. additional controller to manage, adds AWS API dependency
- Secrets Store CSI Driver: secrets as files, no etcd persistence vs. more complex pod spec, SPIFFE/SVID integration needed for zero-trust
- ConfigMap volume mount: supports config reload without pod restart (via inotify) vs. more complex than env vars, requires app to watch for changes

Anti-patterns:
- Committing Kubernetes Secret YAML with base64 values to Git — base64 is encoding, not encryption; anyone with repo access has the secret
- Creating one ConfigMap for an entire cluster namespace — changes to any key trigger unnecessary pod restarts for unrelated services
- Using Secrets for non-sensitive configuration — not an error but adds unnecessary RBAC complexity
- Not rotating secrets — External Secrets Operator supports automatic rotation; not using it means manual credential rotation
- Storing secrets in container image layers (ENV Dockerfile instructions) — baked into image, not rotatable

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Security Pillar: AWS Secrets Manager + ESO is the EKS Best Practices recommended pattern for secret management
- Operational Excellence: ESO automatic rotation reduces manual secret rotation toil
- Reliability Pillar: KMS envelope encryption for etcd satisfies AWS compliance requirements for regulated industries

cleaned_entries.title: Persistent Volumes — Stateful Storage Decisions on EKS
cleaned_entries.content:
Persistent Volumes — Stateful Storage Decisions on EKS

Persistent Volumes (PVs) and Persistent Volume Claims (PVCs) decouple storage from Pod lifecycle. On EKS, PVs are dynamically provisioned by the EBS CSI Driver (block storage) or EFS CSI Driver (shared file system). The storage class chosen determines the AWS storage backing. The critical architectural decision is whether to use in-cluster persistent storage at all — AWS-managed database services (RDS, Aurora, ElastiCache, DynamoDB) are almost always preferable to running stateful databases inside EKS. In-cluster PVs are appropriate for specific use cases: CI/CD runners, ML training data staging, message brokers, search engines.

Decision rules:
- PREFER AWS managed services (RDS, Aurora, ElastiCache, DynamoDB, OpenSearch) over running databases inside EKS — reduces operational complexity, provides automatic backups, Multi-AZ, and managed failover
- USE EBS-backed PVs (gp3 storage class) for stateful workloads that require block storage and run as a single replica: Elasticsearch, Kafka, single-instance databases
- USE EFS-backed PVs for ReadWriteMany (RWX) use cases: shared ML training datasets, CMS media uploads, CI/CD workspace sharing across pods
- USE StatefulSets with volumeClaimTemplates for stateful workloads in Kubernetes — each pod gets its own PVC, guarantees stable pod identity
- SET storage class reclaim policy to Retain (not Delete) for production PVs — prevents accidental data loss when PVC is deleted
- SIZE PVs with 20-30% headroom above current usage — EBS volumes cannot be dynamically shrunk, only expanded

Trade-offs:
- EBS PV: high IOPS, low latency vs. zone-locked (a PV in us-east-1a cannot attach to a pod in us-east-1b), breaks multi-AZ scheduling
- EFS PV: ReadWriteMany, multi-AZ vs. higher latency than EBS (10-20ms vs <1ms), significantly higher cost per GB
- In-cluster database: full control, cost potentially lower vs. you own all operational concerns: backup, failover, upgrades, scaling
- Managed RDS vs. in-cluster PostgreSQL: full-managed, HA, automatic failover vs. managed Postgres can cost 3-5x more for identical specs

Anti-patterns:
- Running production databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL) inside Kubernetes without a deep Kubernetes-native operator like CloudNativePG or Vitess — bare Deployments with PVCs break on node failure
- Using EBS PVs with Deployments (not StatefulSets) with replicas > 1 — EBS is ReadWriteOnce, multiple pods cannot mount the same volume
- Not configuring a VolumeSnapshot schedule for production PVs — EBS snapshots are not automatic, data loss risk on pod/node failure
- Using hostPath volumes in production — data tied to a specific node, breaks scheduler freedom, security risk

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Reliability Pillar: AWS managed databases provide Multi-AZ failover that is extremely difficult to replicate with in-cluster stateful sets
- Operational Excellence: EBS CSI Driver is a required EKS managed add-on — use it instead of the deprecated in-tree AWS storage driver
- Cost Optimization: gp3 EBS is 20% cheaper than gp2 with better baseline performance — always default to gp3 storage class

cleaned_entries.title: Stateless Applications — The Ideal Kubernetes Workload
cleaned_entries.content:
Stateless Applications — The Ideal Kubernetes Workload

Stateless applications are the canonical Kubernetes workload. A stateless application stores no client-specific data locally between requests — all state lives in external systems (database, cache, object storage). Stateless pods are interchangeable, can be killed and rescheduled without data loss, and can be scaled horizontally without coordination. Kubernetes is specifically designed to excel at managing stateless workloads. Web APIs, REST services, GraphQL endpoints, frontend BFFs, and event-driven processors consuming from queues are all stateless patterns that map perfectly to Kubernetes Deployments.

Decision rules:
- CHOOSE Kubernetes for stateless workloads when: multiple replicas are needed, traffic is variable, or there are multiple services with different scaling needs
- USE Deployments with HPA for stateless workloads — pods are interchangeable, rolling updates are safe, horizontal scaling is linear
- ENSURE stateless applications externalize ALL state: use RDS/Aurora for persistent data, ElastiCache for session/cache, S3 for file storage
- CONFIGURE graceful shutdown (SIGTERM handler, terminationGracePeriodSeconds) — pods are terminated routinely and must drain in-flight requests cleanly
- DESIGN for fail-fast startup — stateless pods should be ready in < 30 seconds to enable rapid scale-out during traffic spikes
- WHEN traffic is very low (<100 req/day) and cost is the primary concern, PREFER Lambda over EKS for stateless HTTP handlers

Trade-offs:
- Stateless on EKS: horizontal scalability, resource efficiency vs. requires externalizing all state — adds dependency on RDS/ElastiCache
- Pod count vs. pod size: many small pods (better bin-packing, granular scaling) vs. fewer large pods (simpler operations, less scheduling overhead)
- EKS vs. Lambda for stateless: EKS has no cold start, persistent connections vs. Lambda auto-scales to zero, lower cost for spiky/low traffic

Anti-patterns:
- Storing user session data in pod memory — session lost on pod restart, breaks horizontal scaling (sticky sessions are a workaround, not a solution)
- Using pod-local file system as a temporary data store across requests — use S3 or EFS instead
- Running a stateless application with replicas: 1 — wastes the core value of Kubernetes, single point of failure
- Using EKS for a simple stateless function that runs < 5 minutes on a fixed schedule — CloudWatch Events + Lambda is dramatically simpler

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Performance Efficiency: stateless applications enable horizontal scaling — the Well-Architected pattern for scalable compute
- Reliability Pillar: no local state means pod failure has zero data impact — Kubernetes replaces the pod, service continues
- EKS Best Practices: EKS is designed as a stateless compute platform — stateful concerns are delegated to AWS managed services

cleaned_entries.title: Stateful Applications — StatefulSets, Operators, and the Managed Services Decision
cleaned_entries.content:
Stateful Applications — StatefulSets, Operators, and the Managed Services Decision

Stateful applications maintain data between requests — databases, message brokers, search indices, ML model servers with local weights. Kubernetes can run stateful workloads via StatefulSets, which provide: stable network identities (pod-0, pod-1), stable storage (PVC per pod), and ordered deployment/scaling. However, running production databases inside Kubernetes requires a Kubernetes-native operator (CloudNativePG, Strimzi for Kafka, Redis Operator) that understands the application's failover semantics. The AI agent must evaluate: is the complexity of running this stateful workload on Kubernetes justified, or should it use an AWS managed service?

Decision rules:
- DEFAULT to AWS managed services for stateful data: RDS/Aurora for SQL, ElastiCache for Redis/Memcached, MSK for Kafka, OpenSearch for Elasticsearch
- USE StatefulSet + Kubernetes Operator for stateful workloads ONLY when: the AWS managed service is cost-prohibitive at scale, you need specific database extensions not supported by RDS, or multi-cloud portability is a hard requirement
- NEVER run stateful workloads in Kubernetes without a production-grade operator — bare StatefulSets for databases have no automated failover
- USE StatefulSets (not Deployments) for all workloads requiring stable network identity: Kafka, ZooKeeper, Cassandra, Elasticsearch
- PLAN for PodDisruptionBudgets on StatefulSets — ensure quorum is maintained during node drain, cluster upgrades, and Spot interruptions
- WHEN running Kafka on EKS: prefer Amazon MSK for managed Kafka, reserve self-managed Strimzi only when MSK limits are hit (custom broker configs, extreme throughput)

Trade-offs:
- Managed RDS: fully managed HA, automated backups, Multi-AZ vs. 2-5x more expensive than equivalent self-managed PostgreSQL on EC2/EKS
- Stateful on EKS: cost control, full configuration access vs. you own: backups, failover, upgrades, replication, DR
- Kubernetes Operators: automate complex stateful operations vs. operator bugs can cause split-brain or data loss — maturity matters
- MSK vs. Kafka on EKS: AWS manages brokers, ZooKeeper, TLS vs. lose ability to tune broker JVM, custom MirrorMaker configs

Anti-patterns:
- Running MySQL/PostgreSQL in a bare Kubernetes Deployment with a PVC and single replica — this is a data loss time-bomb, not a production database
- Using Recreate strategy for StatefulSet updates — causes complete database downtime, never appropriate for HA databases
- Not setting up PodDisruptionBudgets for quorum-based systems (Kafka, Cassandra, ZooKeeper) — Kubernetes node drain can take down majority and cause leader election failure
- Mixing stateful and stateless workloads on the same node group — stateful pods with large PVCs cause node-level resource fragmentation

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Reliability Pillar: AWS managed services (RDS Multi-AZ, MSK) provide automated failover that self-managed stateful workloads cannot easily match
- Operational Excellence: choosing managed services reduces operational overhead — reserve StatefulSet complexity for cases where it pays off
- Cost Optimization: detailed TCO analysis required — managed service premium is often justified by reduced engineering hours on DB operations

cleaned_entries.title: REST APIs and GraphQL Services — Scaling Patterns on EKS
cleaned_entries.content:
REST APIs and GraphQL Services — Scaling Patterns on EKS

REST APIs and GraphQL endpoints are the most common EKS workload type. They are inherently stateless, horizontally scalable, and have well-understood traffic patterns. EKS is an excellent platform for API workloads when: the API has consistent traffic, needs multiple microservices, or requires fine-grained scaling control. The key architectural decisions are: Ingress configuration, HPA metrics selection (CPU, custom metrics from Prometheus), connection pooling to backing databases, and circuit breaker patterns for inter-service calls.

Decision rules:
- USE EKS for API workloads when: > 3 independent services, sustained traffic (> 100 req/min baseline), team manages the container platform centrally
- USE Lambda for API workloads when: traffic is highly spiky or near-zero at rest, API response latency tolerance > 1 second, request duration < 15 minutes
- USE ECS Fargate for API workloads when: team wants managed containers without Kubernetes operational overhead, and microservices complexity is moderate (< 10 services)
- CONFIGURE HPA on CPU (70% target) as the baseline autoscaling metric for API pods — add custom metrics (requests-per-second from ALB via KEDA) for more accurate scaling
- IMPLEMENT connection pooling (PgBouncer for PostgreSQL, connection pool in app code) — pod count × max_connections must not exceed database max_connections limit
- SET up pod disruption budgets to maintain minimum available replicas during rolling updates — prevents momentary API unavailability during deploy

Trade-offs:
- EKS vs. Lambda for APIs: EKS has no cold start, persistent DB connections vs. Lambda scales to zero, lower cost at low traffic
- HPA CPU-based scaling: simple, zero-dependency vs. CPU is a lagging indicator — traffic spike may kill existing pods before new ones are ready
- HPA RPS-based scaling (KEDA): scales ahead of traffic vs. requires KEDA operator, Prometheus metrics pipeline, more complex setup
- Microservices API on EKS: independent deployability, scaling, fault isolation vs. distributed tracing required, inter-service latency adds up

Anti-patterns:
- Running a high-traffic API (> 10k RPS) on Lambda — cold starts, concurrency limits, and 15-minute timeout constraints make ECS/EKS a better fit
- Not implementing circuit breakers between microservices — one slow downstream service causes cascading failures across all API callers
- Exposing internal service-to-service APIs via LoadBalancer Service (external IP) — adds latency, cost, and attack surface; use ClusterIP + gRPC/HTTP2 internally
- Deploying all API services in the same namespace with no network policies — any compromised pod can reach all other services

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Performance Efficiency: HPA with ALB request metrics (via KEDA) enables proactive scaling before pod CPU climbs
- Reliability Pillar: PodDisruptionBudgets and minReadySeconds ensure rolling updates maintain minimum API availability
- Security Pillar: ALB WAF + network policies create defense-in-depth for public-facing API workloads

cleaned_entries.title: Background Workers — Queue Consumers and Async Processors
cleaned_entries.content:
Background Workers — Queue Consumers and Async Processors

Background workers process messages from queues (SQS, Kafka, RabbitMQ) or events asynchronously. They are stateless, long-running, and often CPU/memory intensive. On EKS, background workers run as Deployments and scale based on queue depth rather than CPU. KEDA (Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaling) is the standard EKS add-on for scaling workers based on SQS queue depth, Kafka consumer group lag, or Redis list length. Background workers are an ideal EKS workload because they can scale from 0 to many replicas without affecting a user-facing SLA.

Decision rules:
- USE Deployments for background workers — they are stateless consumers; each pod processes independent messages
- USE KEDA (Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaler) to scale worker replicas based on queue depth — SQS queue length, Kafka lag, or Redis list length are the correct scaling signals
- CONFIGURE KEDA minReplicaCount: 0 for cost-critical background workers — pods scale to zero when queue is empty, scale up when messages arrive
- PREFER EKS for background workers when: the worker is CPU/memory-intensive (video encoding, ML inference, PDF processing), runs for > 15 minutes, or needs GPU access
- PREFER Lambda for background workers when: processing time < 15 minutes, event volume is very spiky, and compute intensity is low
- SET appropriate SQS visibility timeout = 2x maximum processing time — prevents message reprocessing when a pod is slow but not failed

Trade-offs:
- KEDA scale-to-zero: eliminates idle worker cost vs. cold start latency when queue fills after idle period (pod startup time 30-90s)
- EKS workers vs. Lambda consumers: EKS can run for hours, uses any language/runtime vs. Lambda 15-minute limit, cold start on burst
- Single worker deployment vs. multiple specialized workers: simpler operations vs. different message types may need different resource profiles

Anti-patterns:
- Scaling background workers on CPU — CPU doesn't reflect queue backlog, pods idle with high queue depth while CPU is low
- Not implementing dead-letter queues (SQS DLQ) — poison messages that crash workers will loop indefinitely
- Running background workers without resource limits — a processing bug (infinite loop, memory leak) can OOM-kill the node
- Sharing the same node group with latency-sensitive API pods — bursty worker CPU usage causes noisy-neighbor latency spikes on API pods

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Cost Optimization: KEDA scale-to-zero for SQS consumers eliminates idle compute cost — core Well-Architected cost optimization pattern
- Reliability Pillar: SQS DLQ + KEDA retry logic ensures no message loss on worker pod failure
- EKS Best Practices: KEDA is an EKS-supported add-on (available via EKS add-on marketplace) for event-driven scaling

cleaned_entries.title: Batch Jobs — CronJobs, One-Shot Jobs, and Long-Running Compute
cleaned_entries.content:
Batch Jobs — CronJobs, One-Shot Jobs, and Long-Running Compute

Batch workloads run to completion rather than serving ongoing traffic. Kubernetes provides two primitives: Job (run-once) and CronJob (scheduled, recurring). Jobs are appropriate for database migrations, report generation, data transformation pipelines, and ML training runs. CronJobs are appropriate for nightly ETL, scheduled reports, cache warming, and cleanup tasks. For large-scale parallel batch processing (Spark, Argo Workflows, data processing pipelines), EKS is the primary platform. For simple, infrequent batch tasks, AWS Batch (managed) or Lambda (short-duration) may be simpler.

Decision rules:
- USE Kubernetes Job for batch tasks that: run for > 15 minutes, need GPU, require specific container images/environments, or are part of a complex DAG (Argo Workflows)
- USE CronJob for scheduled recurring tasks — set concurrencyPolicy: Forbid to prevent overlapping runs when previous job is still running
- USE AWS Batch instead of Kubernetes Jobs when: the batch system team wants managed job scheduling without Kubernetes operational overhead, and jobs are independent (no DAG dependencies)
- USE Lambda for batch tasks when: duration < 15 minutes, triggered by S3 events or EventBridge schedules, and compute is lightweight
- SET activeDeadlineSeconds on all Jobs — prevents zombie jobs from running indefinitely and consuming cluster resources
- USE ttlSecondsAfterFinished on Jobs to auto-clean completed pods — prevents completed job pod accumulation cluttering the cluster

Trade-offs:
- Kubernetes Jobs vs. AWS Batch: full Kubernetes ecosystem integration vs. AWS Batch is managed, no node/scheduler management
- CronJob vs. EventBridge + Lambda: CronJob runs inside EKS (direct cluster access, shared VPC) vs. Lambda is serverless, no idle cost, but 15-minute limit
- Argo Workflows: powerful DAG orchestration, Kubernetes-native vs. significant complexity, requires dedicated operator and UI
- Spot instances for batch Jobs: 70% cost reduction vs. Spot interruption requires job checkpointing or idempotent retry design

Anti-patterns:
- Running batch Jobs on On-Demand nodes when jobs are interruptible — Spot instances are ideal for batch compute (Spot interruption gives 2-minute warning)
- CronJob without resource limits — scheduled jobs running at midnight can starve Spot nodes and impact daytime workloads
- Not setting backoffLimit on Jobs — failed jobs retry indefinitely, burning cluster resources and flooding logs
- Using Deployment instead of Job for finite-work tasks — Deployments restart completed containers, creating infinite retry loops

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Cost Optimization: Spot node groups dedicated to batch workloads reduce batch compute cost by 60-70% vs. On-Demand
- Operational Excellence: ttlSecondsAfterFinished prevents cluster state accumulation — keeps control plane responsive
- EKS Best Practices: separate batch node groups from application node groups via node labels/taints — prevents batch-app resource contention

cleaned_entries.title: Rolling Updates — Zero-Downtime Default Strategy
cleaned_entries.content:
Rolling Updates — Zero-Downtime Default Strategy

Rolling update is Kubernetes' default Deployment strategy. It incrementally replaces old Pods with new ones, ensuring a configurable number of healthy replicas are always running. It is the correct strategy for the vast majority of web services, APIs, and background workers. The critical parameters — maxUnavailable and maxSurge — directly control the trade-off between update speed and availability. In EKS, rolling updates integrate with the ALB's target group health checks — the ALB only routes traffic to ready pods, making zero-downtime deploys achievable without additional orchestration.

Decision rules:
- USE RollingUpdate as the default deployment strategy for all stateless HTTP services — it requires no additional infrastructure
- SET maxUnavailable: 0, maxSurge: 1 for production API workloads — guarantees zero downtime, slightly slower rollout
- SET maxUnavailable: 25%, maxSurge: 25% for background workers where brief capacity reduction is acceptable — faster rollout
- COMBINE rolling update with readinessProbe — new pods only receive traffic after passing readiness checks, protecting users from partially-started instances
- USE minReadySeconds: 10 to prevent premature rollout completion — Kubernetes waits this long after a pod becomes ready before marking it available
- VERIFY backward compatibility before rolling out — during a rolling update, old and new pod versions run simultaneously; APIs must handle both client versions

Trade-offs:
- maxUnavailable: 0 (zero downtime): no capacity reduction vs. requires Surge = extra node capacity to host the new pod before removing the old
- Fast rollout (high Surge): minimizes deployment window vs. higher temporary resource consumption
- Rolling update: simple, built-in, no extra infrastructure vs. both versions run simultaneously — requires API backward compatibility

Anti-patterns:
- Setting maxUnavailable: 1 when total replicas = 1 — this kills the single pod before a replacement is ready, causing downtime
- Not testing the rollback path — rolling updates can be reverted with kubectl rollout undo; this must be validated before production use
- Deploying a version that is not backward-compatible with the stored database schema — during rolling update, new pods may read data written by old pods
- Setting unrealistically short readiness probe timeouts — causes pods to fail readiness, blocking the rollout indefinitely

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Reliability Pillar: rolling update with readiness probes and ALB health checks provides zero-downtime deploys — core AWS deployment reliability pattern
- Operational Excellence: built-in rollout history (revisionHistoryLimit) and rollback support align with EKS operational best practices
- EKS Best Practices: combine Deployment rolling update with ALB target group deregistration delay (draining) to prevent in-flight request drops

cleaned_entries.title: Blue/Green Deployment — Full Version Swap with Instant Rollback
cleaned_entries.content:
Blue/Green Deployment — Full Version Swap with Instant Rollback

Blue/Green deployment runs two complete, identical environments (Blue = current, Green = new) simultaneously. Traffic is shifted from Blue to Green in a single cutover, and Blue is kept running for instant rollback. On EKS, Blue/Green is implemented by: maintaining two Deployments (blue, green) behind a single Service, and switching the Service selector between them; OR using weighted target groups on an ALB to shift 100% of traffic in one step. Blue/Green eliminates the simultaneous-version risk of rolling updates but doubles resource consumption during the transition window.

Decision rules:
- USE Blue/Green WHEN: the application cannot run two versions simultaneously (database schema changes that are not backward-compatible, breaking API changes)
- USE Blue/Green WHEN: instant rollback capability is a hard requirement — switching a Service selector is faster than waiting for a rolling update to reverse
- IMPLEMENT Blue/Green on EKS via ALB weighted target groups (managed by AWS Load Balancer Controller) — shift traffic by changing annotation weights, not kubectl hacks
- KEEP the Blue environment running for a minimum of 30 minutes after Green cutover — observe error rates and latency before decommissioning
- AUTOMATE Blue/Green in CI/CD — manual cutover is error-prone under pressure; use Argo CD or Spinnaker to manage the promotion
- AVOID Blue/Green for background workers consuming from SQS — use a different strategy (drain queue before deploy) since queue consumers are not traffic-switched

Trade-offs:
- Blue/Green: instant rollback, clean version transition vs. doubles resource cost during transition window
- Blue/Green vs. Rolling: no simultaneous versions vs. rolling is resource-efficient and requires zero extra setup
- ALB-based Blue/Green: cloud-native, no extra controllers vs. limited to HTTP traffic — gRPC and WebSocket require NLB consideration
- Kubernetes-native selector swap: fast, free vs. requires two Deployment objects to manage, namespace clutter

Anti-patterns:
- Running Blue/Green for stateless APIs with backward-compatible changes — rolling update achieves the same result with half the resource cost
- Keeping Blue running for days after Green cutover — doubles compute cost unnecessarily; define a decommission SLA
- Using Blue/Green without a database migration strategy — if Green uses a new DB schema, Blue cannot be reactivated without schema rollback
- Switching the Service selector manually via kubectl in production — any typo causes immediate outage; always use GitOps for selector changes

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Reliability Pillar: Blue/Green with ALB weighted target groups is an AWS Well-Architected deployment pattern for mission-critical services
- Operational Excellence: automated Blue/Green via Argo Rollouts + AWS Load Balancer Controller is EKS Best Practices recommended
- Cost Optimization: size the Green environment with minimal replicas until validation is complete — then scale before full cutover

cleaned_entries.title: Canary Deployment — Progressive Traffic Shifting with Automated Promotion
cleaned_entries.content:
Canary Deployment — Progressive Traffic Shifting with Automated Promotion

Canary deployment routes a small percentage of production traffic to the new version, incrementally increasing it while monitoring error rates, latency, and business metrics. If anomalies are detected, traffic is automatically rolled back to 100% stable. On EKS, canary is implemented by: Argo Rollouts (Kubernetes-native, CNCF project) combined with ALB weighted target groups or Istio traffic splitting. Canary is the most sophisticated deployment strategy — it provides real-user validation before full rollout, dramatically reducing the blast radius of bad deployments.

Decision rules:
- USE Canary for high-traffic, user-facing services where even 5 minutes of degraded experience at 100% traffic is unacceptable
- IMPLEMENT Canary via Argo Rollouts on EKS — it replaces the Kubernetes Deployment controller and adds automated promotion/rollback logic
- DEFINE canary success metrics BEFORE deploying: error rate < 1%, p99 latency < 500ms, conversion rate within 5% of baseline — automated promotion is based on these
- START canary at 5-10% traffic weight — only increase (20% → 50% → 100%) after each step passes success metrics for a defined interval
- INTEGRATE Canary with Prometheus + Argo Rollouts analysis templates — automated rollback triggers on metric threshold breach
- AVOID Canary for backend-only changes (no user traffic) — use rolling update; Canary value is highest when real user impact is measurable

Trade-offs:
- Canary: real-user validation, minimal blast radius vs. significant operational complexity — requires Argo Rollouts, Prometheus, metric analysis setup
- Canary vs. Blue/Green: Canary catches issues with real traffic incrementally vs. Blue/Green provides faster cutover with no gradual ramp
- Automated canary promotion: removes human latency from deployment flow vs. requires rigorous metric definition — wrong metrics cause premature promotion or unnecessary rollback
- Service mesh canary (Istio): precise traffic control, mTLS vs. Istio operational overhead may outweigh canary benefits for simpler architectures

Anti-patterns:
- Using canary without automated rollback metrics — manual canary monitoring defeats the purpose; someone must watch dashboards 24/7
- Setting canary traffic to 50% immediately — defeats the purpose of gradual validation; start at 5% and increase stepwise
- Canary without feature flags — canary splits traffic by request, but without feature flags, all 5% canary users see the new feature even if it's not ready for general availability
- Applying canary strategy to database migrations — the canary app version and stable app version must both be compatible with the same DB schema

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Reliability Pillar: automated rollback on metric thresholds is the AWS Well-Architected recommendation for production deployment safety
- Performance Efficiency: Prometheus-driven canary analysis detects p99 latency regression before 100% rollout — preserves user experience SLA
- EKS Blueprints: Argo Rollouts is listed as a recommended EKS add-on for advanced deployment patterns

cleaned_entries.title: EKS vs. ECS vs. Lambda — The Master Compute Decision Framework
cleaned_entries.content:
EKS vs. ECS vs. Lambda — The Master Compute Decision Framework

This is the most critical decision the AI Infrastructure Agent must make. AWS offers three primary container/serverless compute platforms: EKS (managed Kubernetes), ECS (managed containers, Fargate or EC2), and Lambda (serverless functions). Each has a distinct operational model, cost structure, and fitness for different application profiles. The wrong choice leads to either over-engineering (EKS for a simple CRUD app) or under-provisioning (Lambda for a CPU-intensive, long-running service). This entry encodes the complete decision matrix.

Decision rules:
- CHOOSE EKS WHEN: application has > 5 microservices with independent scaling requirements, team has Kubernetes expertise, multi-cluster federation is needed, or advanced deployment patterns (canary, service mesh) are required
- CHOOSE EKS WHEN: workload needs GPU compute (ML inference, training), specialized node configurations, or custom Kubernetes operators
- CHOOSE ECS Fargate WHEN: team wants managed container orchestration without Kubernetes complexity, application has 2-10 services, and there is no existing Kubernetes investment
- CHOOSE ECS EC2 WHEN: cost is the primary constraint, workloads are compute-intensive and Fargate's per-vCPU cost is prohibitive, or workloads need placement control (GPU, large memory instances)
- CHOOSE Lambda WHEN: workload is event-driven, duration < 15 minutes, traffic is highly spiky or near-zero at rest, and functions are stateless
- CHOOSE Lambda WHEN: application profile is a simple monolith with < 1000 req/day — ECS or EC2 is overkill, Kubernetes is extreme overkill
- REJECT EKS WHEN: team has no Kubernetes experience and the workload does not justify the learning investment — ECS Fargate is the correct entry point
- REJECT EKS WHEN: only 1-2 services exist — Kubernetes cluster overhead (control plane cost $72/month minimum, add-ons, operational burden) exceeds the value

Trade-offs:
- EKS: maximum control, rich ecosystem, vendor-neutral Kubernetes API vs. highest operational complexity, 6-12 month learning curve for teams new to Kubernetes
- ECS Fargate: fully serverless containers, AWS-native, simple ops vs. proprietary AWS API, limited to ECS abstractions, less ecosystem tooling
- Lambda: zero operational overhead, scales to zero, pay-per-invocation vs. cold starts, 15-minute timeout, 10GB memory limit, no persistent connections
- EKS cost: control plane $72/month + node groups vs. Lambda pay-per-invocation (can be dramatically cheaper at < 1M invocations/month)
- ECS vs EKS: ECS is faster to adopt, EKS provides portability and richer ecosystem — the right choice depends on team maturity and multi-cloud strategy

Anti-patterns:
- Choosing EKS because Kubernetes is popular — it is the right tool for complex, multi-service, high-scale workloads, not a status symbol
- Running a single-service monolith on EKS — you pay $72/month minimum for the control plane plus node costs for no microservices benefit
- Using Lambda for a workload that maintains persistent WebSocket connections or needs to run for hours — Lambda is fundamentally incompatible
- Using ECS Fargate for GPU workloads — Fargate does not support GPU; use EKS with GPU node groups or EC2 directly
- Choosing Lambda for a high-traffic API (> 10k RPS sustained) — concurrency limits and cold starts become significant operational concerns

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Well-Architected Framework: choose the right compute service for the workload profile — over-engineering is a Well-Architected anti-pattern
- EKS Best Practices: EKS is positioned as the enterprise Kubernetes platform for complex, multi-team, multi-service environments
- AWS Compute Optimizer: for existing workloads, use AWS Compute Optimizer to validate right-sizing before migrating to EKS

cleaned_entries.title: AWS Load Balancer Controller — ALB and NLB Management from Kubernetes
cleaned_entries.content:
AWS Load Balancer Controller — ALB and NLB Management from Kubernetes

The AWS Load Balancer Controller is a Kubernetes controller that watches Ingress and Service resources and provisions AWS ALB/NLB resources accordingly. It replaces the deprecated in-tree AWS cloud provider load balancer integration. It is a required add-on for production EKS clusters. Key capabilities: IngressGroup (share one ALB across many Ingress resources), IP mode target registration (routes directly to pod IPs, bypassing node-level kube-proxy), and native integration with ACM for TLS, WAF for threat protection, and Cognito for authentication. It is managed via Helm and requires an IRSA role with permissions to manage ELB resources.

Decision rules:
- INSTALL AWS Load Balancer Controller as a required Day-1 add-on on every EKS cluster — it is the only supported way to provision ALB/NLB in production
- USE IP target type (alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/target-type: ip) — routes directly to pod IPs, bypasses NodePort, reduces hop count and latency
- USE IngressGroup (alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/group.name) to share one ALB across all HTTP services in the cluster — critical cost optimization
- ATTACH ALB to WAFv2 Web ACL for public-facing services — one annotation enables AWS managed rule groups
- USE NLB Service type for: gRPC services, TCP-level protocols, services requiring static IPs (IP whitelisting by downstream clients)
- CONFIGURE target group deregistration delay to match your application's request drain time — prevents in-flight request drops during pod termination

Trade-offs:
- IP target mode: lower latency, direct pod routing vs. requires VPC CNI plugin (aws-vpc-cni), uses more VPC IP addresses
- Shared ALB (IngressGroup): cost efficient vs. shared failure domain — a routing misconfiguration can affect all services on the group
- ALB vs. NLB: ALB provides L7 features (host/path routing, WAF, Cognito) vs. NLB provides lower latency, static IP, UDP support

Anti-patterns:
- Using the legacy in-tree AWS cloud provider for load balancer provisioning — deprecated, will be removed, does not support modern features
- Not using IngressGroup — 10 Ingress resources = 10 ALBs = 10x ALB hourly cost (minimum $16/month each)
- Setting ALB health check path to / — use the application's dedicated health endpoint (/health, /ping) to avoid serving health check traffic to the app
- Not setting deletion protection on shared ALBs — accidental Ingress deletion deletes the ALB and disrupts all services in the IngressGroup

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- EKS Best Practices: AWS Load Balancer Controller is the recommended and AWS-supported method for ELB management on EKS
- Security Pillar: WAFv2 integration via Load Balancer Controller annotations provides zero-code threat protection for all HTTP services
- Cost Optimization: IngressGroup + IP target mode eliminates per-service NLB/ALB and removes NodePort hop overhead

cleaned_entries.title: IRSA — IAM Roles for Service Accounts
cleaned_entries.content:
IRSA — IAM Roles for Service Accounts

IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) is the EKS mechanism for granting AWS API permissions to Kubernetes pods without using long-lived IAM credentials. It works by associating a Kubernetes ServiceAccount with an IAM Role via OIDC federation. When a pod uses the annotated ServiceAccount, the pod's containers receive short-lived, auto-rotated AWS credentials via the AWS SDK credential chain. IRSA is the fundamental security primitive for EKS — it replaces node-level IAM instance profiles (which grant all pods on a node the same permissions) with fine-grained, per-workload IAM policies.

Decision rules:
- USE IRSA for every pod that needs AWS API access (S3, SQS, DynamoDB, Secrets Manager, ECR) — never use access keys in environment variables
- CREATE one IAM role per service, not one role per cluster — IRSA enables least-privilege per workload
- ENABLE OIDC provider on the EKS cluster during provisioning — required for IRSA to function
- ANNOTATE the Kubernetes ServiceAccount with the IAM role ARN: eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn
- RESTRICT IAM trust policy conditions to the specific namespace and service account name — prevents other pods from assuming the role via IRSA
- USE separate roles for read-only and read-write access to the same resource — reduces blast radius if a pod is compromised

Trade-offs:
- IRSA: fine-grained, auto-rotating credentials, no secrets to manage vs. requires OIDC setup, Terraform complexity for IAM trust policies
- Node instance profile: simple setup vs. all pods on the node share the same IAM permissions — violates least privilege
- IRSA vs. EKS Pod Identity (AWS-native replacement): Pod Identity is simpler to configure vs. IRSA is more widely documented and supported in older EKS versions

Anti-patterns:
- Storing AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY in Kubernetes Secrets and injecting into pods — static credentials, no automatic rotation, high blast radius on compromise
- Granting AdministratorAccess to an EKS node group instance profile — all pods on all nodes have full AWS account access
- Not restricting IRSA trust policy to specific namespace+service account — any pod in the cluster can assume the role
- Creating one IRSA role for the entire application — breaks least-privilege when one microservice needs S3 access and another needs DynamoDB

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Security Pillar: IRSA implements the Well-Architected principle of using temporary credentials with automatic rotation
- EKS Best Practices: IRSA is the EKS-recommended IAM pattern — explicitly preferred over instance profiles in the EKS Security Best Practices Guide
- Operational Excellence: IRSA eliminates secret rotation toil — no more IAM key rotation schedules

cleaned_entries.title: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) — Reactive Workload Scaling
cleaned_entries.content:
Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) — Reactive Workload Scaling

HPA automatically scales the number of pod replicas in a Deployment or StatefulSet based on observed metrics: CPU utilization, memory utilization, or custom metrics (HTTP requests per second, queue depth via KEDA). HPA operates at the pod level — it does not provision new nodes (that is Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter's job). HPA and Cluster Autoscaler/Karpenter work together: HPA creates pending pods, Karpenter/CA sees pending pods and provisions new nodes. The scaling pipeline is: traffic spike → HPA adds pods → pods are pending (no node capacity) → Karpenter provisions a node → pods schedule.

Decision rules:
- USE HPA for all stateless workloads that need to handle variable traffic — it is the primary Kubernetes horizontal scaling mechanism
- SET CPU target utilization at 60-70% for latency-sensitive APIs — lower target gives more headroom before new pods are needed
- SET CPU target at 80% for batch workers where some latency on scaling is acceptable
- USE KEDA (Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaler) for queue-based workers — HPA cannot natively read SQS depth or Kafka lag
- SET minReplicas: 2 for production HTTP services — single pod is a SPOF; HPA minimum ensures HA even at low traffic
- AVOID HPA on StatefulSets when replicas have different roles (Kafka brokers, DB replicas) — HPA adds generic replicas, which may not match quorum requirements

Trade-offs:
- CPU-based HPA: simple, no external dependencies vs. CPU is a lagging indicator — traffic spike may saturate existing pods before new ones are ready
- Custom metrics HPA (KEDA): proactive scaling based on business signals vs. requires Prometheus or KEDA, more complex setup
- High minReplicas: always-available capacity vs. idle cost during low traffic periods
- HPA + Karpenter: elastic scale from 2 to 100+ pods without pre-provisioning nodes vs. new node provisioning adds 60-120s lag to first pod schedule

Anti-patterns:
- Setting both HPA and manual replicas management — HPA will fight kubectl scale commands; let HPA own replica count entirely
- HPA minReplicas: 1 for a public-facing API — during a rolling update, 1 pod terminating + 1 pod starting = momentary zero-capacity window
- CPU target 90% for latency-sensitive services — by the time scale-out triggers, existing pods are under severe stress causing user-facing latency spikes
- Not setting HPA on background workers consuming from SQS — queue depth grows unbounded during traffic bursts

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Performance Efficiency: HPA implements the Well-Architected principle of auto-scaling based on demand — eliminates over-provisioning
- Cost Optimization: HPA + Karpenter enables right-sized node provisioning — nodes match workload demand rather than peak
- EKS Best Practices: HPA + metrics-server is the recommended autoscaling baseline for all production EKS workloads

cleaned_entries.title: Cluster Autoscaler vs. Karpenter — Node Provisioning Strategy
cleaned_entries.content:
Cluster Autoscaler vs. Karpenter — Node Provisioning Strategy

When HPA creates pods that cannot schedule (Pending state), the cluster needs more nodes. Two tools handle this on EKS: Cluster Autoscaler (CA) and Karpenter. CA is the traditional Kubernetes node autoscaler — it scales pre-defined Auto Scaling Groups. Karpenter is the AWS-native, next-generation node provisioner — it watches unschedulable pods and provisions optimal EC2 instances directly (bypassing ASGs). AWS strongly recommends Karpenter as the default for new EKS clusters. Karpenter provisions faster (<60s vs. 3-4 minutes for CA), selects instance types dynamically, and natively consolidates underutilized nodes.

Decision rules:
- CHOOSE Karpenter for all new EKS clusters — it is AWS-developed, open-source, faster, and more cost-efficient than Cluster Autoscaler
- CHOOSE Cluster Autoscaler when: migrating an existing cluster with complex ASG configurations, or when Karpenter's EC2 API permissions are restricted by your organization's SCP policies
- CONFIGURE Karpenter NodePools to include both Spot and On-Demand instances — Karpenter selects Spot when available, falls back to On-Demand on interruption
- ENABLE Karpenter's Consolidation feature — it continuously replaces underutilized nodes with smaller, cheaper instances without manual intervention
- SET Karpenter NodePool resource limits (max CPU, max memory) to cap maximum cluster cost — prevents runaway scale-out events
- EXCLUDE critical system pods (CoreDNS, metrics-server) from consolidation via do-not-disrupt annotations — prevents disruption of essential cluster services

Trade-offs:
- Karpenter: fast provisioning (<60s), dynamic instance type selection, automatic consolidation vs. newer (less battle-tested in some enterprise environments), requires direct EC2 API permissions
- Cluster Autoscaler: mature, widely deployed, works with any Kubernetes distribution vs. slow (3-4 min), cannot mix instance types in a single ASG, no consolidation
- Spot instances via Karpenter: 60-80% cost reduction vs. Spot interruption requires graceful shutdown and rescheduling — workloads must tolerate 2-minute eviction notice
- Aggressive consolidation: maximum cost efficiency vs. consolidation triggers pod migrations — may cause brief disruption for sensitive workloads

Anti-patterns:
- Running Cluster Autoscaler and Karpenter simultaneously — they will conflict on node scaling decisions; choose one
- Not setting Karpenter NodePool CPU/memory limits — a bug in HPA can cause Karpenter to provision hundreds of nodes and generate massive AWS bills
- Using only On-Demand instances in Karpenter NodePool for batch workloads — Spot provides identical compute at 70% savings for interruptible workloads
- Disabling Karpenter consolidation in production — idle nodes accumulate at 50%+ utilization gaps, wasting significant compute spend

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Cost Optimization: Karpenter Spot integration + consolidation is the AWS-recommended node efficiency pattern — can reduce EC2 compute cost by 40-70%
- EKS Best Practices: Karpenter is the AWS-developed, EKS-recommended node provisioner for all new clusters
- Sustainability Pillar: Karpenter consolidation improves cluster bin-packing — fewer nodes = lower energy footprint

cleaned_entries.title: EKS Managed Node Groups vs. EKS Fargate — Compute Plane Strategy
cleaned_entries.content:
EKS Managed Node Groups vs. EKS Fargate — Compute Plane Strategy

EKS offers two compute plane models: Managed Node Groups (EC2 instances managed by AWS in your account) and EKS Fargate (serverless pods — AWS manages the underlying compute, fully invisible to the customer). Managed Node Groups give full control over instance types, storage, GPU, and networking. Fargate abstracts all node management but adds constraints: no DaemonSets, limited storage options, higher per-vCPU cost, and slower pod startup. The decision depends on workload requirements, team operational model, and cost profile.

Decision rules:
- USE Managed Node Groups as the default compute plane for production EKS — maximum flexibility, supports DaemonSets, GPU, local NVMe, and Spot
- USE EKS Fargate for: batch Jobs and CronJobs that should not consume cluster node capacity, or lightweight workloads where node management overhead is undesirable
- USE EKS Fargate ONLY when: workload has no DaemonSet requirement, uses no hostPath/hostNetwork, and pod startup time of 60-90 seconds is acceptable
- AVOID Fargate for: latency-sensitive APIs (slower cold start), GPU workloads, DaemonSet-based logging agents, and stateful workloads needing large EBS volumes
- PREFER Managed Node Groups + Karpenter over Fargate for cost-sensitive production workloads — Karpenter Spot often beats Fargate pricing by 50%
- USE Fargate profiles for dev/test workloads to eliminate node group management overhead in non-production environments

Trade-offs:
- Managed Node Groups: full control, supports all Kubernetes features, lower cost with Spot vs. you manage node OS updates (AWS handles via managed update, but you schedule it)
- Fargate: zero node management, per-pod billing, perfect isolation vs. 30-50% higher cost vs Spot, no DaemonSets, slower startup, 20GB ephemeral storage max
- Bottlerocket (OS for Managed Nodes): minimal attack surface, fast boot, CIS-hardened vs. limits in-node debugging tools (no package manager)
- AL2023 (Amazon Linux 2023): full ecosystem, familiar tooling vs. larger OS footprint vs. Bottlerocket

Anti-patterns:
- Running all workloads on EKS Fargate to avoid node management — Fargate pricing and constraints make it unsuitable as the primary compute plane for complex clusters
- Using self-managed node groups (manually managed EC2 Auto Scaling Groups) instead of Managed Node Groups — you lose AWS-managed node updates, health remediation, and EKS version alignment
- Not enabling Managed Node Group update config for maximum unavailability — default is 1, which slows cluster upgrades significantly for large node groups
- Running EKS control plane without any node compute strategy — control plane costs $72/month; if no nodes, workloads cannot schedule

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- EKS Best Practices: Managed Node Groups are the recommended compute plane — AWS manages node lifecycle, version updates, and health replacement
- Security Pillar: Bottlerocket OS for node groups provides CIS-hardened, minimal attack surface vs. general-purpose Amazon Linux
- Cost Optimization: Managed Node Groups + Karpenter Spot typically achieves 40-60% cost reduction vs. EKS Fargate for sustained workloads

cleaned_entries.title: Resource Requests and Limits — QoS Classes and Scheduling Accuracy
cleaned_entries.content:
Resource Requests and Limits — QoS Classes and Scheduling Accuracy

Resource requests tell the Kubernetes scheduler how much CPU/memory to reserve on a node. Resource limits cap the maximum a container can consume. Together, they determine the pod's Quality of Service (QoS) class: Guaranteed (requests = limits), Burstable (requests < limits), or BestEffort (no requests/limits). QoS class determines eviction priority under node memory pressure — BestEffort pods are evicted first. Correct resource configuration is the foundation of cluster stability. On EKS with Karpenter, accurate requests also determine correct node instance type selection — if requests are too low, Karpenter provisions nodes that are too small and workloads OOM-kill.

Decision rules:
- ALWAYS set both CPU and memory requests for every container — pods without requests are BestEffort and are the first to be evicted under memory pressure
- SET resource requests based on observed p75 usage from production metrics — not p95 or max (too wasteful) and not guesses
- SET memory limits = memory requests for critical pods (Guaranteed QoS) — prevents OOM kill surprises, ensures scheduler reservation matches actual usage
- SET CPU limits only for batch workloads that must not burst — for API pods, consider omitting CPU limits to allow CPU bursting on underutilized nodes (EKS Best Practices recommends this)
- USE LimitRange admission controller to set namespace-level default requests/limits — prevents new deployments from running without resource configuration
- USE Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) in recommendation mode to continuously suggest right-sized requests based on actual usage

Trade-offs:
- Guaranteed QoS (requests = limits): predictable performance, no eviction vs. wastes resources if actual usage is consistently below limits
- Burstable QoS (requests < limits): efficient resource utilization, allows CPU bursting vs. pod can be evicted under pressure, CPU throttling risk
- Omitting CPU limits: allows CPU bursting on idle nodes vs. a runaway process can consume all node CPU, causing noisy-neighbor impact
- VPA in auto mode: automatic right-sizing vs. VPA requires pod restarts to apply new requests — disruptive for stateless APIs

Anti-patterns:
- Setting requests very low and limits very high (e.g., request 10m CPU, limit 4 CPU) — Karpenter provisions a small node, pod OOM-kills on first traffic spike
- Setting memory limits lower than memory requests — Kubernetes immediately kills the pod (invalid configuration)
- Not using LimitRange in production namespaces — one developer deploys a pod without requests, creating a BestEffort pod that OOM-kills during a traffic spike
- Using identical resource profiles for all services — an ML inference container and a lightweight API proxy have wildly different resource needs

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Performance Efficiency: accurate resource requests enable correct Karpenter node sizing — prevents over-provisioning and under-provisioning
- Reliability Pillar: Guaranteed QoS prevents critical workloads from being evicted under node memory pressure
- EKS Best Practices: explicitly recommends omitting CPU limits for latency-sensitive workloads to allow CPU bursting on spare node capacity

cleaned_entries.title: Health Checks — Liveness, Readiness, and Startup Probes
cleaned_entries.content:
Health Checks — Liveness, Readiness, and Startup Probes

Kubernetes uses three probe types to determine pod health. Liveness probe: if it fails, Kubernetes restarts the container — use for detecting deadlocks or hung processes. Readiness probe: if it fails, the pod is removed from Service endpoints and receives no traffic — use for detecting when the app is not ready to serve (dependent service unavailable, cache warming). Startup probe: allows slow-starting containers extra time before liveness kicks in — use for JVM applications, ML model loading, or any app with > 30 second startup time. Incorrectly configured probes cause either infinite pod restarts (liveness too aggressive) or traffic routed to unhealthy pods (readiness too lenient).

Decision rules:
- ALWAYS configure a readiness probe for every HTTP service — this is what prevents traffic from reaching pods during startup and graceful shutdown
- CONFIGURE a liveness probe for long-running services — detects deadlocks; set initialDelaySeconds generously (30-60s) to avoid restart loops during normal startup
- USE a startup probe for applications with > 30 second startup time — prevents liveness probe from killing the container while it is still starting
- USE HTTP GET probe for HTTP services, TCP socket probe for TCP services, exec probe (command) only as a last resort — exec probes create subprocesses and add overhead
- SET probe timeoutSeconds based on 99th percentile response time of the health endpoint — not the p50 — avoid false failures under load
- IMPLEMENT separate /health (liveness), /ready (readiness), and /startup endpoints in the application — each should check different conditions

Trade-offs:
- Aggressive liveness probe (short period, low failureThreshold): rapid recovery from deadlock vs. risk of restart loop on momentary slow responses under traffic spike
- Lenient readiness probe: fewer false positives vs. pods serve traffic before truly ready, causing errors for first N requests
- Startup probe: allows JVM warmup vs. longer time to detect a pod that is stuck and will never start
- Exec probe: can check app-specific conditions vs. creates OS subprocess per check interval, adds overhead on high-pod-count clusters

Anti-patterns:
- Using the same endpoint for both liveness and readiness — if the app is under load and readiness fails (correct behavior), liveness also triggers a restart (incorrect)
- Setting initialDelaySeconds too low for liveness — Kubernetes kills the pod before it finishes starting, triggering a restart loop that looks like an application crash
- No readiness probe on an API Deployment — during rolling update, pods receive traffic immediately on container start before the app has initialized its connection pool
- Liveness probe calling an external dependency (database, third-party API) — if the dependency is down, every pod in the cluster restarts simultaneously

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Reliability Pillar: readiness probes are the mechanism that makes ALB target group health checks meaningful — ALB routes only to ready pods
- EKS Best Practices: configure readiness probe before liveness; prefer HTTP probes; set appropriate thresholds based on p99 response time
- Operational Excellence: startup probe eliminates false-positive restarts during deployments — reduces MTTR noise

cleaned_entries.title: Observability — Metrics, Logs, and Traces on EKS
cleaned_entries.content:
Observability — Metrics, Logs, and Traces on EKS

Production EKS observability requires three pillars: metrics (Prometheus + Grafana or CloudWatch Container Insights), logs (FluentBit to CloudWatch Logs or OpenSearch), and traces (AWS X-Ray or OpenTelemetry). Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus (AMP) and Amazon Managed Grafana (AMG) are the AWS-native managed replacements for self-hosted Prometheus/Grafana. The EKS Add-on for CloudWatch Observability deploys the CloudWatch agent and FluentBit as a DaemonSet, collecting node-level metrics and container logs automatically. The AI agent must select the observability stack based on team expertise, budget, and existing AWS service usage.

Decision rules:
- USE Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus (AMP) + Amazon Managed Grafana for new EKS clusters — eliminates Prometheus/Grafana operational overhead
- USE CloudWatch Container Insights for teams already invested in the CloudWatch ecosystem — provides node, pod, and container metrics with minimal setup
- DEPLOY FluentBit as a DaemonSet for log shipping — it is resource-efficient, supports multiple log outputs, and is the AWS-recommended log collector for EKS
- ENABLE AWS X-Ray for distributed tracing — instrument SDKs in application code, use X-Ray daemon sidecar or OpenTelemetry Collector as a DaemonSet
- SET Prometheus scrape intervals to 30s for production — 15s is only needed for high-cardinality troubleshooting and doubles storage cost
- DEFINE SLOs (Service Level Objectives) for each service: target error rate < 0.1%, p99 latency < 200ms — alert on SLO burn rate, not individual metric thresholds

Trade-offs:
- AMP + AMG: fully managed, scales automatically vs. higher cost than self-hosted Prometheus, AWS-locked observability stack
- Self-hosted Prometheus: full control, open-source, no vendor lock vs. requires storage management, HA setup, retention policies — significant operational overhead
- CloudWatch Container Insights: zero setup for basic metrics, native AWS integration vs. limited query language (CW Logs Insights is not PromQL), higher cost at scale
- OpenTelemetry Collector: vendor-neutral, future-proof instrumentation vs. more complex setup than AWS-specific X-Ray SDK

Anti-patterns:
- Not collecting container-level metrics (only node metrics) — node metrics hide pod-level resource exhaustion and application-level errors
- Using kubectl logs for production debugging — no persistence, no search, no aggregation; use CloudWatch Logs or OpenSearch
- Setting Prometheus retention to 30 days on EKS cluster storage — Prometheus TSDB is not designed for long-term storage; use Thanos, Cortex, or AMP remote write
- Alerting on every individual metric threshold — creates alert fatigue; alert on SLO burn rate (error budget consumption) instead

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Operational Excellence: CloudWatch Container Insights + FluentBit is the AWS-native, minimal-setup observability stack for EKS
- EKS Best Practices: use Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus and Amazon Managed Grafana for production-grade metrics at scale
- Reliability Pillar: SLO-based alerting on error budget burn rate is the Well-Architected approach to reducing alert noise

cleaned_entries.title: RBAC — Role-Based Access Control for EKS
cleaned_entries.content:
RBAC — Role-Based Access Control for EKS

Kubernetes RBAC controls what API actions subjects (users, groups, service accounts) can perform on which resources. On EKS, RBAC integrates with IAM via the aws-auth ConfigMap (legacy) or EKS Access Entries (new, recommended). IAM entities (users, roles) are mapped to Kubernetes RBAC groups or cluster-level permissions. The EKS Best Practices Guide emphasizes: one IAM role per purpose, separate cluster admin from developer access, use namespaced Roles (not ClusterRoles) for application teams, and audit all RBAC bindings regularly. Kubernetes service accounts used by pods should have minimal RBAC — ideally no Kubernetes RBAC permissions at all, just IRSA for AWS API access.

Decision rules:
- USE EKS Access Entries (not aws-auth ConfigMap) for new clusters — Access Entries are API-driven, auditable, and managed via IaC without manual ConfigMap editing
- MAP IAM roles to Kubernetes RBAC groups — never map individual IAM users; roles are manageable and auditable
- GRANT application teams namespace-scoped Roles (not ClusterRoles) — developers should deploy to their namespace, not see other namespaces
- RESERVE system:masters group (cluster admin equivalent) for the platform team IAM role only — no CI/CD pipelines should have cluster admin
- GRANT CI/CD pipeline IAM roles only the RBAC permissions needed: create/update/delete Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps in specific namespaces — not get nodes, list secrets cluster-wide
- USE kubectl auth can-i --as system:serviceaccount:namespace:sa-name to audit what permissions a service account has before deploying

Trade-offs:
- EKS Access Entries: API-driven, Terraform-manageable vs. new feature, some organizations' legacy tooling may not support it yet
- aws-auth ConfigMap (legacy): widely documented, battle-tested vs. manual editing can corrupt the ConfigMap and lock out all cluster access
- Broad ClusterRole: simple initial setup vs. violates least-privilege, one misconfigured service account can read cluster secrets
- Namespace-scoped Roles: strict isolation vs. more Terraform/YAML to manage per team/namespace

Anti-patterns:
- Editing aws-auth ConfigMap manually in production — a YAML indentation error can lock all IAM users out of the cluster, requiring EC2 console rescue
- Granting developers cluster-admin — they can read secrets in all namespaces, delete cluster-critical resources, and elevate privileges
- Using the default service account with no explicit permissions and no automountServiceAccountToken: false — the default SA has no permissions but its token is auto-mounted and can be used to query the Kubernetes API
- Not auditing RBAC regularly — unused bindings accumulate over time, increasing the blast radius of a compromised service account

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Security Pillar: EKS Access Entries + IAM role mapping implements the AWS principle of using IAM for identity and Kubernetes RBAC for authorization
- EKS Best Practices: EKS Access Entries replace aws-auth ConfigMap — AWS-managed, auditable, safe from manual editing errors
- Operational Excellence: Terraform-managed Access Entries create an auditable, version-controlled RBAC configuration

cleaned_entries.title: Network Policies — Pod-to-Pod Traffic Isolation
cleaned_entries.content:
Network Policies — Pod-to-Pod Traffic Isolation

By default, all pods in a Kubernetes cluster can communicate with all other pods — no isolation. Network Policies are Kubernetes resources that define which pods can communicate with which other pods and external endpoints. They are enforced by the CNI plugin. On EKS, two options exist: the VPC CNI plugin with Kubernetes Network Policy enforcement (added in EKS 1.25+) and the Calico network policy engine. Network Policies are the primary mechanism for micro-segmentation in EKS — ensuring that a compromised frontend pod cannot directly reach the database pod.

Decision rules:
- IMPLEMENT Network Policies for any cluster running multi-tenant workloads or sensitive data — the default allow-all is not acceptable for production security
- START with a default-deny-all ingress policy in each namespace, then add explicit allow rules — allowlist model is safer than denylist
- USE Network Policies to enforce service-to-service communication contracts: frontend → API allowed, frontend → database denied
- ENABLE EKS native Network Policy enforcement (VPC CNI) for new clusters — it uses eBPF in the kernel, no additional CNI installation required
- USE Calico Network Policy for: existing clusters where VPC CNI enforcement is not available, or when egress Network Policies must restrict DNS/external access by pod
- TEST Network Policies in a staging environment — a misconfigured policy that blocks service-to-service traffic causes silent failures, not errors

Trade-offs:
- VPC CNI native enforcement: no extra CNI to manage, eBPF-based performance vs. newer feature, limited to EKS clusters with VPC CNI ≥ 1.14
- Calico: mature, rich policy language, works across distributions vs. additional DaemonSet to manage, Calico-specific CRDs
- Default-deny: strong security baseline vs. can block legitimate traffic if allowlist is incomplete — requires thorough service dependency mapping
- No Network Policies: simple, zero overhead vs. complete east-west traffic freedom, compromised pod can reach all services

Anti-patterns:
- Relying solely on security groups for pod isolation — security groups operate at the ENI level (per-node or per-pod with VPC CNI), not per-Kubernetes-label; network policies provide finer control
- Writing Network Policies only for ingress and ignoring egress — a compromised pod with no egress policy can exfiltrate data to any external endpoint
- Not labeling pods consistently — Network Policies select pods by labels; inconsistent labeling creates unintended policy gaps
- Applying the same Network Policy to all namespaces — different environments (dev, staging, prod) have different trust boundaries

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Security Pillar: Network Policies implement micro-segmentation — the AWS Well-Architected 'defense in depth' pattern at the pod level
- EKS Best Practices: enable Network Policies to complement VPC security groups — Network Policies provide Kubernetes-aware isolation that SGs cannot
- EKS Blueprints: Network Policy enforcement is listed as a required security add-on in EKS production cluster blueprints

cleaned_entries.title: EKS Security Hardening — Pod Security, CIS Benchmark, and Supply Chain
cleaned_entries.content:
EKS Security Hardening — Pod Security, CIS Benchmark, and Supply Chain

Comprehensive EKS security hardening operates at four layers: cluster configuration (control plane logging, private API endpoint, envelope encryption), node security (Bottlerocket OS, IMDSv2 enforcement, no SSH), pod security (Kubernetes Pod Security Standards — Restricted profile, no privileged containers), and supply chain security (ECR image scanning, admission control via OPA Gatekeeper or Kyverno). The EKS Best Practices Security Guide maps each control to the CIS Kubernetes Benchmark v1.8. The AI agent must ensure that security is not an afterthought — it is embedded in the cluster provisioning Terraform and enforced at admission time.

Decision rules:
- ENABLE EKS control plane logging for all log types (api, audit, authenticator, controllerManager, scheduler) — sent to CloudWatch Logs for forensic analysis
- USE private API endpoint for production EKS clusters — the Kubernetes API should not be accessible from the internet; use VPN or bastion for admin access
- ENFORCE IMDSv2 (hop limit 1) on EKS node launch templates — prevents containers from using IMDS to steal node EC2 credentials
- APPLY Pod Security Standards at namespace level: Baseline for most workloads, Restricted for sensitive workloads — enforced via Pod Security Admission (built into Kubernetes 1.25+)
- DEPLOY OPA Gatekeeper or Kyverno for custom admission policies: require image tags (no :latest), require resource limits, require non-root user
- ENABLE ECR image scanning (Enhanced Scanning with Amazon Inspector) for all repositories — block deployments of images with CRITICAL CVEs via OPA/Kyverno admission policy
- ROTATE the EKS cluster certificate annually and when team member leaves — use EKS rotate-certificate API

Trade-offs:
- Private API endpoint: strong security posture vs. requires VPN or bastion for kubectl access — operational complexity for development teams
- Pod Security Standards (Restricted): blocks privileged containers, rootless requirement vs. some third-party add-ons require privileged pods (may need exception namespaces)
- OPA Gatekeeper: powerful policy language (Rego), audit mode vs. Rego has a steep learning curve; Kyverno uses Kubernetes-native YAML and is easier to adopt
- ECR Enhanced Scanning: continuous CVE monitoring vs. Scanner may block deployments on library vulnerabilities that are not exploitable in your context

Anti-patterns:
- Public EKS API endpoint without IP allowlisting — the Kubernetes API is exposed to the internet, any stolen kubeconfig gives full cluster access
- Running containers as root (UID 0) — if a container breakout occurs, the attacker has root on the node
- Allowing :latest image tags in production — non-deterministic, cannot roll back, no image digest pinning
- No admission control — developers can deploy containers with privileged: true, hostNetwork: true, and no resource limits
- Not patching EKS cluster version regularly — EKS versions reach end-of-support; unpatched clusters accumulate CVEs in Kubernetes API server and etcd

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Security Pillar: private API endpoint + control plane logging + IMDSv2 + KMS envelope encryption addresses all four EKS security baselines in the Well-Architected Framework
- EKS Best Practices Security Guide: maps directly to CIS Kubernetes Benchmark v1.8 controls — use this guide as the authoritative security checklist
- EKS Blueprints: Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper, ECR scanning, and private endpoint are all standard components of the EKS Blueprint reference architecture
